KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

High pressure peaks across northern New England through the day
on Thursday, keeping a seasonably cool and dry airmass in 
place. Another radiational cooling night is expected tonight, 
with a frost advisory issued for more interior zones and into 
the MidCoast tonight. Overall tonight looks slightly cooler than
last night through the sheltered valleys, while a breeze keeps 
hilltops warmer. South of these areas along the coastal plain, a
northeasterly breeze overnight keeps any frost isolated and 
patchy. During the daytime, mainly sunny skies with highs in the
60s continue.

While the high brings cool and fair weather to northern New 
England, a developing storm system off the Carolinas continues 
to organize to our south. The surf continues to build over the 
next few days as a long easterly fetch strengthens across the 
North Atlantic between the high overhead and the developing 
storm system. These waves bring increasingly large breaking surf
and rip currents through the end of the week. 


KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

While there are still details to iron out, models have overall come 
into better agreement in the strong coastal low lifting northward 
across the western Atlantic on Friday before slowing down and 
lingering near southern New England through the weekend. Given the 
decreasing spread in the guidance, confidence is increasing that 
this system will likely bring high surf, gusty winds, and a 
soaking/beneficial rain. With astronomical tides on the increase, 
storm surge may also push water levels close to minor flood 
stage near the times of high tide along with splash over.

Confidence remains highest in surf becoming dangerous by Friday as 
incoming swells and a long fetch of northeast winds continue to 
build seas...with large breaking waves and a high risk of rip 
currents along the coast. These conditions will likely last through 
the weekend, potentially requiring a High Surf Advisory.

The pressure gradient will continue to tighten between the incoming 
low and high pressure to the north and west. So regardless of the 
low track, brisk north to northeast winds are likely, most notably 
along the coast. These should start become more noticeable during 
the day Friday, but most guidance has the period of the stronger 
winds spanning from Friday night through Sunday, although the ECMWF 
is a little later as it has slowed lifting the low north. Based on 
latest guidance, 30-40 mph gusts along the coast look reasonable, 
and these could exceed 40 mph at times, especially from Cape 
Elizabeth southward. This could carry a limited power outage threat 
with leaves still on trees. Unless the low tracks farther north, 
winds across the interior should be more in the 20-30 mph range.

A soaking and beneficial rain is looking more likely as the latest 
NBM PoPs bring 60-70% south of the mountains and 70-80% along the 
coast and parts of SE NH. As far as timing, Friday looks to stay 
mostly dry, but rain chances will increase from south to north 
Friday night through Saturday. As far as amounts, ensemble means 
from the ECMWF/GFS (including the ECMWF AIFS/AIGEFS) favor a 
widespread 1-2" south of the mountains with increasing 
probabilities (60-80%) for 2+" along the coast from roughly 
Portland extending south to the Seacoast. Low-level lapse rates 
will be steepening, perhaps enough to allow a small amount of 
instability, and this could produce some convective elements and
higher rain rates at times. As the previous shift mentioned, 
some enhancement is possible from the Seacoast extending into 
coastal Cumberland, with support from the ECMWF ensemble having
10-20% potential for 4 inches of rain on the high end

Lastly, astronomical tides will be trending higher this weekend, and 
models are advertising surge approaching 1.5 to 2 feet, which could 
push water levels close to flood stage along the coast around the 
times of high tide. Splashover is also possible. 

Improving conditions are possible later in the day Monday as the low 
begins to pull away to the east, but the drier conditions are more 
likely by Tuesday of next week, which look to continue into 
Wednesday.
